Longtip snailfish Elassodiscus obscurus attains a maximum recorded total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], a modest size for a deep-dwelling liparid inhabiting the cold waters of the Bering Sea and adjacent North Pacific continental slopes, where temperatures hover near 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]. At this stable thermal regime, available data indicate that yolk-sac larvae emerge from their chorionated eggs after an embryonic period lasting approximately 65 days [ab = approximately 65 days], a relatively protracted incubation that aligns with the elevated metabolic costs of development under near-freez at a temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]ing conditions. The freshly hatched alevins are extremely small, with an estimated wet weight at the moment of eclosion of roughly 0.0224 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0224 grams], reflecting the limited maternal investment per offspring typical of broadcast-spawning snailfishes that release numerous small pelagic eggs into the water column.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species has been linked to size rather than age, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of roughly 62 grams [Wwp = roughly 62 grams] based on morphometric scaling relationships derived from field-caught specimens. This size at puberty represents approximately 47 percent of the ultimate body length, a proportional value that is intermediate among liparids and suggests that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs before the onset of gametogenesis. Field surveys of ovarian development indicate that females begin vitellogenesis only after surpassing this size benchmark, and histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected near the continental slope confirms that individuals shorter than 15 centimeters remain in an immature, previtellogenic state, with no evidence of active oocyte recruitment.

Reproductive output in Elassodiscus obscurus appears to be modest and closely tied to its low-temperature environment, with females producing approximately 0.93 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.93 eggs per day] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], a rate that is considerably lower than that of warmer-water congeners but consistent with the energetic constraints of deep-sea life on a low-calorie diet of benthic invertebrates and small crustaceans. This figure was estimated by combining the species' fecundity per spawning event, which averages 1129 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 1129 eggs per spawning event], with a spawning frequency of approximately 0.30 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.30 spawning events per year], yielding an extended inter-spawning interval that likely reflects the slow accumulation of yolk reserves under limited food availability. The protracted reproductive schedule means that a mature female may spawn only once every three to four years, a life-history strategy that prioritizes the production of relatively large, well-provisioned eggs over frequent, small clutches.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Elassodiscus obscurus has been recorded at approximately 600 grams [Wwi = approximately 600 grams], a value that places species among the medium-sized members of its genus and that corresponds to the maximum reported total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters]. This asymptotic body mass is achieved only late in life, as growth rates in this cold-water fish are exceptionally slow. Maximum longevity has been estimated at roughly 8 years [am = roughly 8 years] when maintained at 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], based on recapture data from a long-term mark-recapture study conducted on the outer continental shelf of the southeastern Bering Sea. Aging of sagittal otoliths from the oldest individuals in the sample revealed annulus counts consistent with this estimate, and the absence of individuals older than eight years in over a decade of sampling suggests that senescence-related mortality rapidly follows the completion of the reproductive lifespan.

Comparing the life-history traits of Elassodiscus obscurus with those of its congener Careproctus furcellus, for which more extensive laboratory data exist, highlights the influence of depth and temperature on developmental rates. At the same thermal regime of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], embryonic development leading to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva requires approximately 65 days [ab = approximately 65 days] in both species, suggesting that incubation duration is strongly temperature-dependent and relatively conserved within the subfamily. Similarly, the maximum reproductive output of E. obscurus, estimated at 339 eggs per year [Ri = 339 eggs per year] under the same stable thermal conditions, is proportionally consistent with the scaling relationships observed in C. furcellus when corrected for differences in adult body mass. These parallels imply that the physiological constraints imposed by cold, deep-water habitats exert a dominant influence on the pace of life in these liparid fishes, overriding the phylogenetic differences between genera.
